action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"); Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
 - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- If the file is outside the working directory, you must use your `Read` tool to read it before editing. This tool will error if you edit such a file without reading it first.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

- Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time
- Use this tool when you need to find files by name patterns
- When you are doing an open ended search that may require multiple rounds of globbing and grepping, use the Agent tool instead (if available)

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
  - Supports full regex syntax (e.g., "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+")
  - Filter files with glob parameter (e.g., "*.js", "**/*.tsx") or type parameter (e.g., "js", "py", "rust")
  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool (if available) for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)
  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

1	# edfringe-now - the data-pipeline checks
2	
3	The `data-pipeline` skill carries the judgment for the edfringe.com scrape
4	(`scraper/`) and the committed data it produces (`data/`, `site/data/`). What has a signature is
5	enforced by a check:
6	
7	- `edfringe-lookup-indices` - every positional reference in the wire files resolves in
8	  `site/data/venues.json`.
9	- `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` - `scripts/verify.sh` runs `normalize.py --selftest`
10	  as a command, not only as a step label.
11	- `edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output` - every file under `data/` and `site/data/` has a
12	  generator's shape.
13	
14	## `edfringe-lookup-indices`
15	
16	`lookup-indices.mjs` asserts that every positional reference in the committed wire files resolves
17	inside `site/data/venues.json`'s lookup lists: the day files' `genre` / `room` / `subs` / `ts` and
18	`shows.min.json`'s `g` / `rm` / `sg` / `ar` / `p[].t` (`-1` is the producer's "unknown" and
19	passes). Its red-first fixture is `data-checks.test.mjs`, run by `npm test` / `scripts/verify.sh`;
20	the last fixture runs the rule over this repo's real committed data, so the check is a live gate on
21	every scrape commit and not just a unit test of itself.
22

Use before touching scraper/, data/, site/data/, the scrape and price tasks, or the site code that decodes, prices or times performances.

21	
22	# The data pipeline
23	
24	The API's field reference is `scraper/SCRAPING.md` and the file layout `scraper/README.md`; this
25	is the judgment those two don't carry.
26	
27	## Verifying a change
28	
29	- **Verifying a scraper change against the live API** — only a sanctioned task drives the
30	  API: `full-scrape`, `fetch-prices`, `price-probe`, `refresh-shows` or `refresh-tickets`. Never
31	  "verify" by reasoning about what the API probably returns; have a task run it, or say plainly
32	  it is unverified.
33	
34	- **Answering a one-off API question** (a field's shape, an enum's values, whether an operation
35	  exists) — `scraper/SCRAPING.md` first; past it, `www.edfringe.com`'s Next.js bundles carry
36	  the client's full GraphQL operation set (recipe in SCRAPING.md), where the probe shows the host
37	  reachable. That shows what a query looks like, never what it returns, so a change checked only
38	  that way is still unverified. Past that, ask the owner.
39	
40	- **Changing the normalizer** — `python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform
41	  check that runs offline (raw → master → day file → `shows.min.json` on a fixture). Run it.
42	
43	## Tickets and prices
44	
45	- **Writing availability logic, client or scraper** — key off the per-performance
46	  `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` with nothing to
47	  sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). `SOLD_OUT` and `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` are
48	  unavailable, everything else available, unknown available (`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in
49	  `site/js/app.js`). `soldOut` is carried for display only.
50	
51	- **Pricing a show** — price every performance, not one per show: previews sell cheaper and
52	  weekends dearer, and pricing one performance published 28% of shows at their cheapest night.
53	  No "skip previews" heuristic fixes that; GraphQL aliases carry a whole run per request
54	  (`fetch_prices.prices_query`), and there is no call budget to economise against.
55	
56	- **Choosing which price a payload carries** — `shows.min.json` (planner) answers "what does
57	  this show cost?" with the run-wide `priceMin`..`priceMax`; `site/data/days/*.json` (Now page)
58	  answers "what does it cost tonight?" with that performance's own `pm`. A performance the cache
59	  has no entry for gets no `pm` at all ("Price TBC"), never a neighbouring night's figure or the
60	  show's minimum.
61	
62	- **Handling a show with no price** — it is a normal, permanent state: `data/prices.json` is a
63	  fetch-once cache off the nightly path, and `refresh-shows` carries its amounts through without
64	  re-fetching. Keep both cache entry shapes readable (current `sets` + `perfs`, legacy bare
65	  `min`/`max`; `price_sets` reads both); dropping the legacy shape or emptying the cache blanks
66	  prices until a full pass finishes.
67	
68	- **Encoding a price at any stage** — keep three states, never two:
69	
70	  | state | master | wire |
71	  |---|---|---|
72	  | costs nothing | `priceMin: 0` | `pm: 0` |
73	  | priced | `priceMin: 22.5` | `pm: 22.5` |
74	  | unknown | `priceMin: null` | no `pm` key at all |
75	
76	  Never encode unknown as `0` or let a decoder default it to one. `priceMin: 0` and `free: true`
77	  are separate claims (the flag is the listing's, the £0 can be the price API's); the price path
78	  keys off `priceMin` and `free` stays what the listing said. What the site shows for an unknown
79	  price is a product decision in `site/shared/price.js`.
80	
81	- **Reading the raw price payload** — amounts arrive as strings, and nearly every show carries a
82	  £0.00 "Personal Assistant" concession that is never the cheapest price (SCRAPING.md's pricing
83	  section).
84	
85	## Time
86	
87	- **Reading a performance's `dateTime` from the listing API** — it is a real UTC instant, not
88	  Edinburgh wall-clock with a decorative `Z`; slicing its digits is an hour wrong all August. The
89	  pipeline crosses the zone once, in `normalize.local_date_start`, shared by
90	  `refresh_ticket_status.py` and `fetch_prices.py`. Everything written after it is Edinburgh
91	  wall-clock, so no stage downstream parses, converts or re-offsets a time.
92	
93	- **Comparing "now" against performance times** — read now in Edinburgh too,
94	  `site/js/clock.js`'s `festivalNow` / `festivalDate`, never the device clock: a UK visitor can't
95	  see the difference, a visitor from another zone gets the whole drift. (now-compared-against)
96	
97	- **Changing the time-zone conversion** — it is a full-snapshot change: rebuild the master
98	  through the new conversion and regenerate every derived artifact. Expect performances to move
99	  between day files (late 31 Aug ones fall into 1 Sep, outside the August day files) rather than
100	  reading that as data loss. (conversion-change-full)
101	
102	## Committed data and caching
103	
104	- **Fixing wrong data under `data/normalized/` or `site/data/`** — fix `scraper/normalize.py`
105	  and re-run it (`--merge` to top up, no flag for a full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit
106	  is overwritten by the next `refresh-shows` and leaves the bug in the generator.
107	  `data/prices.json` is committed input written by `scraper/fetch_prices.py`, and nothing
108	  overwrites a hand-edit there, which is why re-running the fetch is the only fix.
109	
110	- **Adding a festival, an edition or a source** — `site/data/festivals/` is
111	  `scraper/convert/to_serving.py`'s output and `data/festivals/` its hand-fetched input; name each
112	  new file and its writer in `edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output`'s allowlist, never the
113	  directory.
114	
115	- **Writing a job that commits generated data and can run over an hour** — its push is
116	  guaranteed to be rejected by the hourly ticket refresh, so on rejection re-derive rather than
117	  merge: fetch `origin/main`, take its generated files, regenerate from that master plus the
118	  job's own input, retry. Call `commit_regenerated` in the task workers' `worker-lib.sh`, which
119	  does exactly that.
120	
121	- **Changing anything that moves a performance's join key** (venue + date + time) — the
122	  browser caches `shows.min.json` and `availability.min.json` separately and joins them by that
123	  key, so a generation split breaks the join while both files are fresh by TTL.
124	  `join_fingerprint(master)` in `normalize.py`, mirrored as `joinFingerprint()` in
125	  `site/plan/lib/hydrate.js` and carried as the sidecar's `k`, is how `plan.js` detects the split
126	  and evicts both. Keep the two implementations agreeing (the self-test asserts it); a TTL bump
127	  doesn't cover this.
128	
129	## The wire format
130	
131	- **Adding or dropping an indexed wire field** — the day files and `shows.min.json` reference
132	  `site/data/venues.json`'s lists by position (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`,
133	  `ar`), with one producer and two decoders that change in the same commit: `scraper/normalize.py`
134	  (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` / `minify_master` / `build_availability`),
135	  `site/js/app.js` `adaptShow`, and `site/plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`.
136	  `edfringe-lookup-indices` catches an unresolved index but not a decoder reading the old key, so
137	  check both decoders by hand.
138	
139	- **Changing a lookup list** — append only (`extend_lookup`), never reorder or drop: the browser
140	  decodes a days-old catalogue against a newer `venues.json`, and a moved entry relabels shows
141	  with no error anywhere. (lookup-lists-append)
142	
143	- **Putting anything that changes through the day into `shows.min.json`** — don't: ticket status
144	  lives in `availability.min.json` so `refresh-tickets` rewrites it alone; in the catalogue it
145	  would tie that bulky download to the refresh and freeze availability in cached copies.
146	  `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`. (shows-min-json)
147	
148	- **Adding a plain wire key** (such as `pm` / `px`) — the same three files move, and the new key
149	  sits at the same position in `normalize_event`'s dict and `rehydrateShows`'s object literal:
150	  the round-trip test compares as JSON, so a key-order mismatch fails it and reads like a data
151	  bug.
152

1	---
2	name: requirements-harness
3	description: How EdFringeNow runs product/requirements.md as tests under a real headless Chromium - writing leaves and goldens, the harness's determinism traps, the frozen fixtures and golden approval. Use before editing product/requirements.md or anything under product/requirements/.
4	metadata:
5	  body: guidelines
6	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
7	    - "product/requirements.md"
8	    - "product/requirements/**"
9	---
10	
11	# The requirements harness
12	
13	The framework conventions are the `executable-requirements` pack and the judgment layer is
14	`spec-driven-product` plus the `writing-tests` skill; layout, lanes and commands are
15	`product/requirements/README.md`. This carries what those don't: a Playwright golden harness,
16	and the local approval and fixture policy.
17	
18	## Writing the spec
19	
20	- **Laying out `product/requirements.md`** — under each visual leaf its golden is visible and
21	  uncollapsed; every textual expansion (acceptance notes, proof pointers) is collapsed in a
22	  `<details>` block. The document is read by sight.
23	
24	- **Writing a visual leaf's statement** — one line saying what is asserted; the golden carries
25	  the copy, counts, colours and placement. Anything not visible (a threshold, the rule behind
26	  the state) goes in a collapsed **Notes** block. (visual-leafs-statement)
27	
28	- **Choosing a golden's capture** — the smallest surface that proves the leaf: an element crop,
29	  a clipped region, or a stitched composite, never the whole page or control. The recipe lives on
30	  the case (`capture: "<selector>"` or `capture(page, tools)`, see `shared/capture-tools.js`);
31	  whole-page capture is a deliberate exception. (golden-smallest-surface)
32	
33	- **Proving what an action changes** — capture the same region before and after (and after a
34	  reload where persistence is the point) and play them as one animated golden (`tools.animate`);
35	  keep `stitchV`/`stitchH` for things genuinely side by side. (change-time-animation)
36	
37	- **Encoding an animated golden** — APNG, never GIF (`shared/png.js`'s `encodeAnimated`); the
38	  comparator compares an animated golden's bytes only. (animated-golden-apng)
39	
40	- **Placing a leaf both pages follow** — the spec is organised by what the product does, never by
41	  code layout: a cross-page rule is one feature whose picture shows both the Now page and the
42	  planner, in the cross-page part after the two page-by-page segments. A case may navigate
43	  between pages, or open a second page when something fixed at context creation must differ.
44	
45	- **About to route a leaf to `behavior` or `logic`** — first ask whether it decomposes into
46	  observable states; a statement joined by "and" usually does, and each part becomes its own
47	  numbered sub-leaf with its own picture, the parent a heading. When a leaf lands in a coded kind
48	  because the product makes it invisible, say so in its Notes and name the product change that
49	  would make it visual.
50	
51	- **Using `behavior`** — for a gesture's outgoing consequence (a URL built, bytes downloaded,
52	  storage written) or what the OS paints rather than the page (a native `title` tooltip, a
53	  cursor). (behavior-rule)
54	
55	- **Using `logic`** — for a pure rule with no rendered surface; when it is about how values are
56	  written, declare `table: { columns, rows }` so the gallery renders the table and `verify()`
57	  proves every row. (logic-rule)
58	
59	## The browser is part of the expected
60	
61	- **Bumping the pinned Playwright** — it re-renders every golden, so it is a re-baselining,
62	  approved like one: the harness refuses any other version (`shared/harness/browser.js`).
63	
64	- **A comparison that flaps** — add determinism, never a tolerance; the comparator stays at zero
65	  diff, and the levers (fixed clock, geolocation, seeded `Math.random`, route-fulfilled network,
66	  frozen animations, render flags) all live in the harness.
67	
68	## Traps the harness already paid for
69	
70	- **Serving the fake origin** — keep it `https://`: geolocation exists only on secure origins,
71	  and on plain http the app keeps its simulated clock and renders the wrong day.
72	  (geolocation-exists-only)
73	
74	- **Moving or denying the fixed geolocation** — the app adopts the device clock only on an
75	  in-UK fix, so anywhere else renders its pre-set simulated moment, a different day file.
76	  (app-adopts-device)
77	
78	- **Captures racing the planner's board animation** — a CSS freeze doesn't stop
79	  `element.animate`; the harness stubs it to land on end states. (css-freeze-does)
80	
81	- **Text shifting by a pixel everywhere** — the vendored `fonts.css` resolves against
82	  `fonts.googleapis.com`, so the vendor route matches on path, host-agnostic. (fonts-arrive-google)
83	
84	- **Adding an emoji, symbol or script to the product or fixtures** — rebuild the
85	  `harness/vendor/systemfonts/` subset (its README): Chromium runs under a `FONTCONFIG_FILE`
86	  that sees only that directory, and a missing glyph renders as tofu. (vendoring-web-fonts)
87	
88	- **Reproducing a golden flake locally** — compare with the harness's `compare.js`, never a byte
89	  hash: PNG bytes differ across identical renders, and CI enforces pixels.
90	  (reproducing-golden-flake)
91	
92	- **A red `ui-requirements` lane** — its artifact downloads from a host the proxy denies, so read
93	  which case failed from `get_job_logs` (large `tail_lines`) and re-run it locally;
94	  `npm run test:ui` writes `.actual.png` / `.diff.png` into `shared/.artifacts/`. (red-ci-lanes)
95	
96	- **Capturing a floating popup** — set `viewportOnly: true`: a full-page capture scrolls, and
97	  scrolling dismisses tips, legends and pops. (floating-popup-dies)
98	
99	- **Waiting for a page to be ready** — wait on the observable state the pages settle into (the
100	  footer version popup's text, the search placeholder's show count; `case-helpers.js`) plus
101	  `document.fonts.ready`, never `networkidle`. (ready-networkidle)
102	
103	- **Capturing hover-driven UI** — open it inside `capture()`, not `drive()`: the runner settles
104	  the scroll between them, and the scroll fires `mouseleave`. (hover-driven-ui)
105	
106	## The fixture freeze
107	
108	- **Needing data for a case** — use `shared/fixtures/data/`, a frozen snapshot of the real
109	  committed data cast by the committed builder for state variety; never reach for `site/data/`.
110	  Every deviation from the source bytes is an `ADJUST` in the builder.
111	
112	- **Re-running the builder** — it re-casts every golden, so run it only with the owner's
113	  approval and land builder, fixtures, goldens and gallery in one reviewed change.
114	
115	- **Having invoked `build-fixtures.js` at all**, even against a scratch edit — it writes into
116	  `fixtures/data/` as it goes, so `git diff --stat` the whole fixtures dir before deciding there
117	  is nothing to revert. (build-fixtures-partial-drift)
118	
119	## Golden approval
120	
121	- **A golden that no longer matches** — show the owner the committed golden beside
122	  `shared/.artifacts/<case>.actual.png` and `.diff.png` through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, one
123	  per item, and say so in the PR body.
124	
125	- **Landing an intended UI change** — spec edit (doc-first, red), then the implementation, then
126	  `npm run refresh:ui`, with the refreshed PNGs in the same diff.
127

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A schema property** — when the lesson is about a document's *shape*: a field that must be present, a
59	   value from a closed set, a type, a key set nothing may extend. It belongs in the JSON Schema the document
60	   points at with `$schema` (created from the first such rule where the document has none), which an editor
61	   shows while the document is written and the engine's `schema-conformance` check enforces for every such
62	   document at once. Anything a schema can enforce is better handled there: a declared `checkParsedFiles`
63	   assertion over a field, or a coded rule re-reading a document's shape by hand, is a schema check in
64	   disguise. Only what a schema cannot say — a relation between two documents, a value that depends on the
65	   tree — goes on to the rungs below.
66	2. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
67	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. Declare it at the moment its signature
68	   lives: a **world** check over the tree — one pass ("these patterns over these files"), or two when a value
69	   read in one place must agree with, exist in or be absent from another (`extractValueSets` derives the set,
70	   `checkSetValues`/`checkSetPairs`/`requireIdenticalFiles` quantify over it); a **work** check over the
71	   change (`scope: "work"` — the lines it adds or removes, a co-change, an untracked file, the session's
72	   declared comment classes); or an **action** guard on a tool call (`scope: "action"`, `guardToolCalls` —
73	   denied or nudged at PreToolUse, backstopped over the transcript at Stop). Most captured conditions are
74	   one of these, and a lesson about *how an operation is performed* is usually the third. Give it
75	   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
76	   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
77	   else's next change, not this run's.
78	3. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
79	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
80	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
81	   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
82	   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
83	4. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure or a bias rather than a condition —
84	   and name the moment it must load under its `metadata`: `force-load-on-file-edits-paths`,
85	   `force-load-on-tool-calls` (opening a PR, committing, merging, fetching), `force-load-on-prompts-matching`
86	   (an owner's command phrase) or `force-load-on-tool-results-matching` (a symptom in a result). A skill
87	   with no trigger loads on description alone, which is model discretion; a procedure keyed to an act has a
88	   call to name, and rules sharing a trigger belong in one skill so one load carries the whole procedure.
89	5. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
90	
91	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
92	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
93	both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
94	[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
95	
96	**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
97	exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
98	derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).
99	
100	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
101	relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small** — a pass adds at most two rules, each one
102	sentence. How a rule is phrased and sized, and where its rationale goes — the brief rule in `RULES.md`, the
103	reaffirmable reason on the rule's provenance file - is the
104	[writing-pack-prose](skills/writing-pack-prose/SKILL.md) skill's; load it before writing any. The full
105	evidence trail stays in the PR body and the issue.
106	
107	When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
108	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
109	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
110	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
111	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
112	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
113	
114	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
115	trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
116	run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
117	rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
118	basics pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
119	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
120	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
121	
122	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
123	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
124	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
125	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
126	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
127	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
128	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
129	
130	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
131	
132	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
133	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
134	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
135	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
136

1	# edfringe-now — this repo's own rules
2	
3	Lessons this repo paid for once. A lesson that would hold in another repo belongs in the
4	Claudinite canon instead. The data pipeline's rules are the `data-pipeline` skill and the
5	requirements harness's are the `requirements-harness` skill; each loads when its paths are edited.
6	
7	## Delivering work
8	
9	- **Asking how to fix a structural or architectural complaint via `AskUserQuestion`** — offer
10	  restructuring itself as one option, not only mechanism-level tweaks to the existing shape; the
11	  owner's free-text answers have named the restructure nobody offered.
12	  (askuserquestion-structural-option)
13	
14	- **Opening a PR for a work item's own issue** (a bot-filed `[claudinite-work]` item or a person's
15	  marked ad-hoc issue) — reference it without `Closes #N`: GitHub's auto-close beats
16	  `converge-item.mjs` and leaves the issue closed but still wearing its live status label.
17	  (never-closes-n-own-issue)
18	
19	- **Writing a PR body** — this repo has no PR template, so write it from the commit message
20	  without searching for one. (no-pr-template)
21	
22	- **Reaching for `verify-in-production` after merging a change to what the site renders or
23	  does** — file nothing: the goldens, `npm run test:ui` and a look at the served page run before
24	  the merge. Reserve it for non-user-facing infra whose effect first appears in a deploy, a
25	  scheduler slot or a CI lane. (verify-in-production-infra-only)
26	
27	- **Writing a duration or before/after number into a commit or PR body** — compute it from real
28	  timestamps, never a felt sense of elapsed time around unconsumed background sleeps.
29	  (measured-duration-real-timestamps)
30	
31	- **Landing a lesson that tells a session to retry, ignore or explain away a permission, security
32	  or classifier denial** — don't, however much retry evidence backs it: a checked-in rule is a
33	  standing bypass every unattended session loads. Report a recurring denial to the owner instead.
34	  (no-denial-bypass-rules)
35	
36	## Verifying a change
37	
38	- **Calling a change under `site/` or the requirements fixtures done** — run `npm run test:ui`
39	  locally: `npm run verify` never compares the goldens, and CI's `ui-requirements` lane skips them
40	  on a diff outside `site/` and `product/`. (test-ui-before-pixel-change)
41	
42	- **Verifying a UI change** — look at it: serve `site/` (not the repo root) with
43	  `python3 -m http.server 8000` and drive `http://localhost:8000` with the preinstalled
44	  Chromium; the pages fetch their data, so a `file://` open fails. For `/plan`, a slug-per-line
45	  text file works as a favourites list. (serve-site-to-look)
46	
47	- **Scripting Playwright** — import the global build by its ESM entry and launch with no
48	  `executablePath`; `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` already points at the matching browser.
49	  (launch-playwright-executablepath)
50	
51	  ```js
52	  import { chromium } from '/opt/node22/lib/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs';
53	  ```
54	
55	- **A bare `import 'playwright'` failing with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`** — use the absolute import
56	  above rather than `npm i playwright`: a fresh install pulls a newer Playwright that wants a
57	  browser build the image doesn't ship, and in the repo root it dirties `package.json`.
58	  (npm-playwright-scratchpad)
59	
60	- **The Now page throwing `L is not defined` under Playwright** — Leaflet loads from `unpkg.com`,
61	  which the browser can't reach here; route `https://unpkg.com/**` to the matching file in
62	  `product/requirements/shared/harness/vendor/leaflet/` before navigating. (site-index-htmls)
63	
64	- **Asserting a driven page logged no errors** — filter failed requests to off-box hosts (Google
65	  Fonts, map tiles, anything the browser can't tunnel to); they fail on every run and are not
66	  application errors. (known-noisy-console)
67	
68	- **A "the live site shows wrong data" report** — ask first for screenshots of DevTools' Network
69	  tab and Application → Cache Storage panel, before building a local repro: three caching layers
70	  can produce the identical symptom, and only the browser's evidence says which is in play.
71	  (live-data-bug-browser-evidence)
72	
73	## The sandbox and its network
74	
75	- **About to report a capability as unavailable** — probe it in this session first, whatever
76	  this file says; the egress policy changes from day to day. (report-capability-unavailable)
77	
78	  ```sh
79	  curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" --max-time 15 https://<host>/
80	  ```
81	
82	- **Reading a 403 from the proxy** — `curl -v` tells you whose it is: `CONNECT tunnel failed,
83	  response 403` is a policy denial, the same code after a negotiated tunnel is the origin
84	  refusing you. `curl -sS "$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status"` lists recent policy rejections.
85	  (reading-403-proxy)
86	
87	- **Checking what the deployed site serves** — `curl https://www.edfringenow.com/…` rather than
88	  reasoning from the working tree, but the response is CDN-cached: re-check after a delay before
89	  reading a stale 200 as a failed deploy. (checking-deployed-site)
90	
91	- **Needing a screenshot of an off-box site headless Chromium can't tunnel to** — route every
92	  request through `page.route('**/*', …)` fulfilled by `curl`, where the probe shows `curl`
93	  reaches the host. (offsite-screenshot-via-curl)
94	
95	- **Building a command or poll on `gh`** — it is not installed here; use the GitHub MCP tools,
96	  and never suppress a poll condition's stderr, which is what would have said so.
97	  (no-gh-cli)
98	
99	## GitHub and CI
100	
101	- **Calling `actions_list` for workflow runs** — always pass `perPage`; without it the call
102	  overflows the tool-result limit on this repo's history. (actionslist-listworkflowruns-overflows)
103	
104	- **Checking whether a PR merged via `list_pull_requests`** — read `merged_at` for non-null; the
105	  `merged` field decodes `false` even for a merged PR. (listpullrequestss-merged-field)
106	
107	- **`pull_request_read method=get_files` overflowing** — retry at a smaller `perPage` (10 works
108	  where 100 overflows), or answer from `get` plus `get_commits`. (pullrequestread-method-getfiles)
109	
110	- **A CI job stuck `queued` until it auto-cancels, or dying in "Prepare all required actions"** —
111	  that is a GitHub outage, not this PR's failure: say what local `verify`/`test:ui` covers, and
112	  don't recommend waiting it out. (ci-infra-outage-tells)
113	
114	- **A `[claudinite-task]` needs-human issue piling up bot comments** — the watchdog is nagging
115	  about one unexecuted slot, not reporting a recurring failure; count what landed
116	  (`git log --grep=<worker's commit subject>`) and read that slot's job log before shipping a fix.
117	  (needs-human-one-slot)
118	
119	## The site's code
120	
121	- **Writing behaviour more than one page needs** — put it in `site/shared/` and import it from
122	  each page; never copy it. `site/plan/lib/`'s DOM-free engine (`engine.js`, `travel.js`,
123	  `itinerary.js`, `availability.js`) is shared with `site/planNG/`, so it never learns one
124	  festival's specifics. (cross-page-in-shared)
125	
126	## Product research and design
127	
128	- **Researching a competitor for a `wiki-growth` pass** — fetch the competitor's page first, and
129	  fall back to `WebSearch` only once the fetch fails, citing the snippet's publisher.
130	  (competitor-fetch-first)
131	
132	- **Dispatching a research subagent for a long, multi-round wiki pass** — give it an explicit
133	  budget ("finish with a few NOT FOUNDs rather than dig exhaustively"): a subagent killed
134	  mid-run hands back no report at all. (research-subagent-budget)
135	
136	- **Building a first-pass UI/UX mockup** — default to graphics-first, minimal-text, wizard-style
137	  screens that hide answered questions; the owner rejects generic buttons-and-prose screens.
138	  (mockup-graphics-first)
139

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 5. get_commits - Get the list of commits on a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 6. get_review_comments - Get review threads on a pull request. Each thread contains logically grouped review comments made on the same code location during pull request reviews. Returns thread metadata and comments with nullable current and original line-range coordinates (line, start_line, original_line, original_start_line). Current coordinates are omitted when unavailable, such as for outdated comments. Use cursor-based pagination (perPage, after) to control results.
 7. get_reviews - Get the reviews on a pull request. When asked for review comments, use get_review_comments method. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 8. get_comments - Get comments on a pull request. Use this if user doesn't specifically want review comments. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 9. get_check_runs - Get check runs for the head commit of a pull request. Check runs are the individual CI/CD jobs and checks that run on the PR.

{"number":863,"title":"Plan the Edinburgh Fringe from the festival planner, proven at its real size","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG?thread=cmsg_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG8MJoqVPN7Kc9sKJC7dAqiG)_

**Before:** the festival planner (`/planNG/`) knew only the Israeli festivals, which have tens of shows each. Nothing proved its lists and draft would survive the Fringe's ~4,000 shows and ~58,000 performances. With the whole Fringe pooled, the venue filter drew 291 options and the page came to 3,352 elements.

**After:** the Edinburgh Fringe is a registered festival that you can focus and plan in planNG. It reads the existing wire files, so there is no new serving file and no wire, cache or join-fingerprint change, and the Now page and `/plan` are unchanged. Haifa, Acco and Jerusalem still never fetch the Fringe files, which the new leaf 25.4 proves. Every list is capped from `limits.js`, and a new `scale` kind asserts those caps and time budgets against the real `site/data/`.

Measured in Chromium, Edinburgh focused:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| DOM elements | 3,352 | 2,051 |
| venue filter options | 291 | 30 (+ "N more") |
| programme list rows | 0 (search-first) | 0 (search-first) |
| search rows | 40 | 40 |
| first render | 806 ms | 842 ms |
| re-draft | 205 ms | 169 ms |
| JS heap | 72 MB | 57 MB |

Haifa, Acco and Jerusalem after the change: first render 312–337 ms, re-draft 10–16 ms, 955–1,070 elements.

### How
- **Registry** (`scraper/festivals/`, `scraper/convert/`): every edition declares a `format`, either `block` or `edfringe-wire`. There is no default. Edinburgh's `festival.toml` maps the Fringe's own files and scripts onto the registry roles. `to_serving.py` lists that edition but refuses to convert it.
- **Adapter** (`site/shared/festival-catalogue.js`): Fringe editions are read through `hydrate.js` into the same shape as a serving block. The Fringe's load, cache and fingerprint-retry code moved from `plan.js` into `site/shared/edfringe-wire.js`, and both pages now call it.
- **Caps** (`site/shared/limits.js`): `FACET_OPTIONS` (30) keeps the busiest venues, `RIVAL_ROWS` (8) caps the rivals list, and each shows a line for the rest.
- **Edinburgh presentation**: wordmark, genre emoji, a magenta theme and UK trip links.
- **Curated venues** (`scraper/festivals/edfringe/curated/venues.json`): room capacities and stage types for the Pleasance Courtyard, Dome and EICC, Gilded Balloon Teviot and the Traverse. Each figure carries its source URL, and a figure nobody published is null. The file is not wired into any served file yet.
- **Spec**: new leaves 23.7 (Edinburgh screen), 25.3 (caps table), 25.4 (lazy loading) and 26.1–26.2 (scale). The harness's pinned clock of 15 Aug falls inside the Fringe, which would make Edinburgh the default festival, so the Part V cases now name `?festival=jerusalem-comedy`.

**Goldens refreshed** (not owner-approved; listed for review):
- `jerusalem-i18n.19.1.png`, `jerusalem-theme.19.2.png`, `planng-timeline.23.1.png`, `planng-theme.23.6.png`: the timeline now includes Edinburgh.
- `planng-edinburgh.23.7.png`: new.
- No Now-page or `/plan` golden changed.

**Findings:**
- The draft on the Fringe is valid, but its picks are questionable: scarcity-first favours one-off Events and Exhibitions.
- The draft is bound by garbage collection. I didn't cache slot eligibility because of the correctness risk.

**Tests:**
- `npm run verify` passes; its only output is the three advisories already on `main`.
- `npm run test:ui` passes locally, 149 of 149. Scale run: first calendar 812 ms, re-draft 173 ms, 2,052 elements.

**Stack:** based on #850 (`claude/project-thread-oxhepr-plan-ng`, which carries #847 and #846), with the Haifa and Acco branches merged in. Merge after #850.

Closes #862

{"number":846,"title":"Jerusalem planner: starred shows obey "how full a day"","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG?thread=cmsg_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG8MJoqVPN7Kc9sKJC7dAqiG)_

Before: on the Jerusalem planner, changing "how full a day" did nothing to starred shows. If you starred the three Sun 18 Oct shows (opening, love-story, kharman) and set at most 1 show a day, all three stayed on Sunday. It looked as if the calendar filters had stopped working.

After: a starred show obeys "how full a day", and it already obeyed your day hours. It still skips the "what you are here for" limit. With the same three stars and 1 show a day, Sunday keeps one show (opening). The other two are offered on the stack or counted as crowded out. Locked shows still ignore all three limits (20.10). The new spec leaf `20.12` is a logic table generated from the drafter. No golden changed.

How: `draftCalendar`'s sweep in `site/plan/lib/contention.js` used one `capped` flag for two separate limits. It now takes two flags, `dayCap` and `tasteCap`. The favourites pass sets `dayCap` and leaves `tasteCap` off. The locks pass leaves both off. Only the Jerusalem page imports this drafter, so the Edinburgh `/plan` page does not change. `contention.test.mjs` no longer pins the old behaviour. It gains cases for a starred show taking one of the capped places, extra starred shows moving to another night, and a lock ignoring the cap. Checked in a real browser against the served page: `npm run verify` passes, `npm run test:ui` 134/134 pass.

Closes #844

{"number":847,"title":"Festival data layer: fetcher → raw per edition/source → converter → serving block (Jerusalem re-homed)","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG?thread=cmsg_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG8MJoqVPN7Kc9sKJC7dAqiG)_

**Before:** Jerusalem was one script (`scraper/jerusalem/fetch.py`) that fetched the site, geocoded venues and wrote the festival-specific `site/data/jerusalem/shows.json` directly. Raw data was never kept, it had no notion of an edition, and a festival could only have one source.

**After:** each festival has a `festival.toml` that declares its editions (the id is the year; the ordinal is a separate field) and its sources, with roles and whether each is required. Hand-run fetchers write only their own `data/festivals/<festival>/<edition>/<source>/` folder, in the site's own vocabulary, with a `manifest.json`. Curated venue research (rooms, seats, layout, with a URL for every figure) lives in `scraper/festivals/<dir>/curated/`. Only the converter (`scraper/convert/`) knows our information requirements. It writes a festival-agnostic serving block per edition to `site/data/festivals/<festival>/<edition>.json`, plus the registry `site/data/festivals/index.json`. Jerusalem is the first festival on this layout. The planner is unchanged: `site/data/jerusalem/shows.json` is still produced, byte-identical, from the same raw.

**How**
- `scraper/convert/merge.py` runs one adapter per source and merges fields by the precedence declared in `[merge]`. It records which source supplied each field (`provenance.fields`) and refuses a source that supplies a section its roles don't cover.
- `schema.py` validates the whole block before anything is written: types, referential integrity, dates within the edition ±1 day, no duplicate ids, and unknown kept as null rather than 0.
- Writes are atomic and limited to the requested edition. A fetch is swapped into place whole, so a failed fetch leaves the previous raw untouched.
- `to_serving.py --check` (added to `verify.sh`) re-derives every committed serving file from committed raw and exits 1 on any drift.
- Jerusalem's raw is re-homed from the committed catalogue, not re-fetched, because the site can't be reached from this session. The manifests say so, and `fetchedAt` is null because the original fetch time was never recorded.
- `site/shared/festival-catalogue.js` loads a serving block into the exact in-memory shape the planner uses today. Its test deep-equals the result against `adaptCatalogue(shows.json)`.
- The contract the Haifa and Acco PRs will follow is in `scraper/festivals/README.md`.

Tests: `npm run verify` green (326 unit tests, plus the parse, converter and fetcher-writer self-tests and `--check`; conformance 0 blocking). `npm run test:ui` green (134/134, goldens unchanged).

Closes #845

{"number":850,"title":"planNG: plan any festival on an open calendar, focused from a year's timeline","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG?thread=cmsg_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG8MJoqVPN7Kc9sKJC7dAqiG)_

**Before:** `/planJerusalem/` planned one festival. Its five nights were hard-wired, and it read a single file of its own.

**After:** `/planNG/` plans any festival in the registry. A full-width timeline of the coming year shows one bar per edition. Choosing a bar sets the planning period to that festival's run plus one day on each side. Buttons at each end of the calendar add a day, up to a 31-day cap.

The calendar drafts from every performance in the period that can be reached from the focused festival's city:
- A festival within a day trip joins the pool whole.
- A distant one joins only for nights outside the focused run and its travel days.
- A festival left out for distance is named on the page.

Other changes:
- **Origin question:** the first time a festival is chosen, the page asks once where the reader is coming from: this city, elsewhere in the country, abroad, or their device's location. The answer decides the trip links. A local reader gets no bed or journey; a domestic one gets a bed and a train; a reader from abroad also gets airport transfers.
- **Theme:** the page takes the focused festival's colours (Jerusalem, Haifa, Acco).
- **List caps:** browse asks for a search when there are more than 100 shows, search shows at most 40 results, and the interest question shows 10 options before a "more kinds" chip.
- **Redirect and migration:** old `/planJerusalem/*` addresses redirect with a 301 to `/planNG/*`. What a reader saved on the old page is carried over once.

**How:**
- New shared modules: `site/shared/feasibility.js` (who can reach what) and `site/shared/limits.js` (the list caps).
- New planNG modules: `site/planNG/lib/{timeline,pool,migrate}.js` and `timeline-view.js`.
- IDs in the combined pool are namespaced `<festival>/<id>`.
- The pre-registry `site/data/jerusalem/shows.json` and the script that wrote it are removed.

**Stacking:** this PR is based on #847 (festival data layer). It also carries #846's commits (calendar cap), merged in, until #846 merges.

**Goldens:** 23 Part V goldens are re-rendered and 3 are new. Every `jerusalem-*` screen golden changed because the calendar now covers the period (two narrow edge days added), and the timeline and origin card now sit above it. New goldens: `planng-timeline.23.1`, `planng-theme.23.6`, `planng-origin.24.1`. All of them appear in the gallery in `product/requirements.md`. The emoji font subset gained 🏠 and 🎬.

Tests: `npm run verify` and `npm run test:ui` pass (143/143, run twice).

Closes #849
