{"number":873,"title":"Convert the scrape and prices workflows to Claudinite tasks","body":"`scrape.yml` becomes the `full-scrape` task. `prices.yml` becomes two tasks: `fetch-prices` (the pricing job) and `price-probe` (its raw-probe job). All three are agentless `trigger: request` tasks that run from a hand-created item. Operator parameters are passed as Context bullets (`per: 50`, `slug: …`, `commit: false`).

**Kept as workflows**
- `ci.yml`: it's the pull-request gate, and a task can't be triggered by a pull request.
- `claudinite-scheduler.yml` and `claudinite-executor.yml`: these are the task engine itself.

**How the conversion works**
- **Kill switch.** The workflows' `if: false` is now the `scraping-switched-on` precondition, set in `tasks/scraping-switch.mjs`. While it's off, a created item declines with the old "switched off" message. `price-probe` stays outside the switch, as `raw-probe` was. I chose a precondition over `taskScheduler.disabledTasks` because `disabledTasks` stops the scheduler from asking but doesn't stop an item somebody creates by hand.
- **The one-hour leash.** The full price pass takes about 2.6 hours, and the executor reclaims code-work after one hour. `fetch_prices.py` gets a new `--time-budget` option. The worker prices for 40 minutes, commits, and then requeues its own item while shows remain.
- **Push retry.** Both workflows had their own copy of the "re-derive on rejected push" loop. There is now one shared `commit_regenerated` in `tasks/worker-lib.sh`. `worker-lib.test.mjs` tests it against a real rejected push.
- **Dropped:** the uploads of the raw pages and the raw-probe payload as artifacts. They were `uses:` steps, which a task can't run. The raw pages are a regenerable cache, and the probe now prints its payload to the run log.

**Notes**
- One historical source line in `provenance/_pack.md` has been trimmed from the deleted path to "the `scrape.yml` workflow". Without that, `reference-integrity` blocks. The trim leaves one advisory from `provenance-change-recorded`.
- Not changed here: `taskScheduler.disabledTasks` in `.claudinite-settings.json` names `edfringe/refresh-shows` and `edfringe/refresh-tickets`, but the pack's id is `edfringe-now`. So those two entries don't match anything.
- Verified: `npm run verify` passes except for the two conformance findings this branch then fixed. After those fixes the task tests (21/21) and the pack tests pass, the world sweep has 0 blocking findings, and `fetch_prices.py --selftest` passes. None of the tasks can be run against the live API while scraping is switched off.

Closes #872

{"number":852,"title":"Add the Acco festival 2026 (theatre + street programmes)","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG?thread=cmsg_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG8MJoqVPN7Kc9sKJC7dAqiG)_

**Before:** the festival registry held only the Jerusalem Comedy Festival. There was no data for Acco.

**After:** `acco` 2026 (27.9–1.10) is registered and served at `/data/festivals/acco/2026.json`. It holds 69 events, 350 performances and 7 venues, across two programme categories:
- The Acco Theatre Centre's פסטיבל תיאטרון עכו: 22 shows, 28 performances.
- The municipality's free מופעי חוצות: 47 items, 322 performances.

The festival's own labels become categories: הפקת מקור, הצגה אורחת, בכורה, הצגות חממה, לנשים בלבד. Sold out becomes `status: sold-out` (2 performances), and free entry becomes `free` at a price of 0. 14 roaming or TBA street items have no times, so they are reported in `provenance.skipped`.

**How:**
- `scraper/festivals/acco/`: `festival.toml`, the curated venue research, and two hand-run fetchers. Each fetcher refuses to write when the page's own year disagrees with `--edition`. Each has a `parse.py --selftest` over committed `samples/`.
- `scraper/convert/adapters/acco/`: where the pages' labels become categories, genre, status, free and price.
- The raw comes from the 2026-09-24 WebFetch research, transcribed into the fetchers' shape, because curl to both hosts is blocked here. Each `manifest.json` says so (`fetcher: "research-2026-09-24"`).
- The samples are reconstructions and are labelled as such.
- Creator names are not landed. Theatre runtimes, halls and prices stay null.
- The README says a hand-run fetch on a machine with egress should replace the raw and the samples.

Stacks on #847.

Closes #851

{"number":853,"title":"Haifa International Film Festival 2026 (42nd) on the festival data layer","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG?thread=cmsg_016GMQY219tD7Ja6gZKX6ZGG8MJoqVPN7Kc9sKJC7dAqiG)_

Before: the festival registry had one festival, the Jerusalem Comedy Festival. The Haifa International Film Festival, which runs 25 Sep – 3 Oct 2026, had no data anywhere in the repo.

After: `haifa-iff` 2026 (the 42nd edition) is in `site/data/festivals/index.json`, and its serving block `site/data/festivals/haifa-iff/2026.json` carries 119 films and 10 events, with 224 performances across 6 venues. The films are filed under 17 section categories (multi-valued). Seven industry sessions are genre `talk`. The flat tariff (49/46/150/115 ₪ plus passes) sits in `festival.ticketing`. The opening event is the only performance with a price (150 ₪), and every status is `unknown` because there is no availability source. The block loads through `adaptFestival`.

How:
- `scraper/festivals/haifa_iff/` holds festival.toml and a hand-run `haifaff-site` fetcher. The fetcher reads the English and Hebrew schedules, the film pages and the event pages, and refuses to write when the site's edition number ("42nd", "ה-42", `Festival: 42`) disagrees with the edition's `ordinal`. There is also a pure `parse.py`, whose `--selftest` runs on samples reconstructed from markdown renderings of the real pages, not captured bytes. The README says this, and the parser reads element kinds, never class names.
- The 2026 raw is a transcription of the 2026-09-24 WebFetch research, because haifaff.co.il is denied at CONNECT here. Its manifest records `fetcher: "research-2026-09-24"` and the known gaps. The first real fetch on a machine with egress should overwrite it.
- Curated venue research gives a URL for every figure. Every coordinate is approximate, because no geocoder was reachable, and each venue's notes say so. Smarticket availability is declared `required = false`, and its fetcher refuses until someone maps the seller's API.
- The adapters are under `scraper/convert/adapters/haifa_iff/`. The raw and serving files are allowlisted by name. verify.sh's `sources/*/parse.py` glob picks up the new self-test.

Stacks on #847 (base `claude/project-thread-oxhepr-festival-data`).

Tests: `npm run verify` is green, including `haifa parse selftest: ok` and `to_serving.py --check` (4 serving files match their raw). `npm run test:ui` passes 134 of 134.

Closes #848

{"number":861,"title":"Claudinite: tasks usage fold","body":"Regenerated `.claudinite/local/tasks-usage.GENERATED.json` from this repo's scheduler and executor run
listings, each run's jobs, the cost records those runs printed, and the work
items that have closed since the last fold.

Per day and per workflow: runs, jobs, billed minutes and — only where this
pack's config carries `actionsMinuteRate` — the spend they imply. Per run: the
API calls it made and its wall time per phase. Per task: what its occurrences
came to, the parks they collected, and the four latency samples their label
events answer.

{"number":822,"title":"Add a dispatch-only raw price probe job to prices.yml","body":"Refs #821

## What changed

Adds a new `raw-probe` job to `.github/workflows/prices.yml`. It runs only
when the workflow's existing `slug` input is filled in (that field already
existed for the full pricing job's single-slug mode, which stays exactly as
inert as before — `if: false` on the `prices` job is untouched). The new job:

- runs `python3 scraper/fetch_prices.py --slug <slug> --print-raw --out /tmp/raw-probe-cache.json`
- writes the raw `performancePrices` payload to the run's step summary and
  uploads it as a downloadable artifact (both, per the issue's "and/or")
- touches no repo file: `--out` points at a throwaway path under `/tmp` on the
  runner rather than `data/prices.json`, and there is no commit or push step
  at all.

No change to `scraper/fetch_prices.py` — its existing `--slug`/`--print-raw`
flags were already exactly what this needs.

## Reading of the ask

The issue's suggested design reused the workflow's dispatch-only shape but
didn't say whether the raw-probe job should get its own input or reuse
`slug`. I reused the existing `slug` input rather than adding a duplicate:
the pricing job's single-slug mode has been dead since it went inert, so
letting a filled-in `slug` select the raw-probe job instead is the smallest
change, and I updated that input's description to say so.

## To answer #294's question

Dispatch this workflow with `slug` set to one of the suggested £3.00-fee
probe targets — e.g. `nathaniel-jones-2-by-2`, `adam-riches-the-critic-s-way`,
or `abandoman-afterglow` — and read the raw payload off the run's step
summary (or the `raw-price-probe-<slug>` artifact). Compare against a
£1.50-fee show (any show not in that list) for contrast. Nothing else needs
to be filled in; `limit`/`batch_size`/`min_delay`/`max_delay`/`commit` are
ignored by this job.

## Left out

No `Automerge:`/`Merge:` field on the work item — this adds a (narrow, opt-in)
path that reaches the live API, so per the issue this PR is opened for review
and not landed automatically. This is why the PR is left open rather than
closing #821: the issue is the work item itself, and its park is the
in-review state until a person merges or closes this PR.

{"number":870,"title":"Provenance: backfill edfringe-now","body":"Closes #869

Backfills the provenance of the local pack `edfringe-now` from its history, using the `backfilling-provenance` method. This comes before cleaning up its RULES.md. No rule, check or task changes.

## Counts
- **35 owed files filled**: 34 were empty, including `_pack.md`, and 1 (`report-capability-unavailable.md`) held only the conversion's entry. `apply --backfill` replaced that placeholder `born` (dated 2026-09-20) with the real birth in #609. It carried over the placeholder's Reason and Retire-when.
- **`_declined.md` created**, with 4 candidates:
  - #85: the "ad-hoc PR has no linked issue" friction. It is canon workflow, not local.
  - #124: the scraper's stdout-buffering fix. The fix belongs at its call site.
  - #402: recovering from a classifier-blocked workflow commit through the API tools.
  - #420: "retry a classifier-blocked push once". This one and the #402 candidate are both route-around-a-denial lessons, which this repo bars.
- `check edfringe-now` now shows no empty or conversion-only file, exit 0.

## Where the brief's derivation was corrected
- **Elements that came from `edfringe-requirements` and `edfringe-data`**: the brief could not trace them back past #613, because it read only the `edfringe` paths. I traced them by hand:
  - The harness rules were born in #316.
  - `red-ci-lanes` was born in #353.
  - `reproducing-golden-flake` was born in #420.
  - `lookup-lists-append` and `shows-min-json` were born in #252.
  - `now-compared-against` and `conversion-change-full` were born in #278.
  - #613 is now recorded as a `moved` on every element that existed then.
- **`logic-rule` and `behavior-rule`**: the brief matched the one-word triggers "logic" and "behavior" to #85 and #353. Both were really born in #316.
- **`checking-deployed-site` and `reading-403-proxy`**: born in #262. #609 reworded them.
- **MCP call-shape rules**: born in #391 (#420 for `get_files`). The #694 revalidation reworded them.
- **Tasks**: born in #101. Policy changes are recorded through #235, #236, #252, #340, #472, #545, #586, #601, #670 and #731.

## Minimal entries (the evidence ran out)
These got a `born` that gives only the carrier and the #316 source, plus their `moved` entry:
- `logic-rule`
- `geolocation-exists-only`
- `css-freeze-does`
- `fonts-arrive-google`
- `vendoring-web-fonts`
- `floating-popup-dies`
- `ready-networkidle`

`now-compared-against` shares only the #278 incident as its Reason. #670's policy changes to both tasks carry no Reason, because the update PR stated none.

113	# Working with generated files
114	
115	- **Working with a file a test or tool generates** — put `GENERATED` in its name, and don't
116	  hand-edit it; change the generator. Never resolve its merge conflict by hand: clear the
117	  markers with either side, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit that
118	  output. Consider automating the clear with a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry, and
119	  `git rerere` for a conflict that recurs.
120	
121	- **A generator whose OWN set of outputs grows on its own** — one baseline per auto-discovered
122	  category (a new test "kind", a new fixture), rather than a fixed, named list — needs its
123	  `merge=ours` coverage to auto-track that growth too, typically a glob or pattern in
124	  `.gitattributes` rather than one entry per file. A per-file allowlist silently stops covering
125	  the moment a new category starts committing its own baselines, and the gap surfaces as a
126	  binary merge conflict git cannot 3-way-merge at all — at the worst possible moment, mid-merge,
127	  for a category nobody remembered to wire up.

132	# Writing pack prose
133	
134	Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
135	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.
136	
137	**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
138	[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
139	principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
140	the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
141	layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.
142	
143	## The ration
144	
145	Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
146	forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.
147	
148	- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
149	  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
150	  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
151	- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
152	  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
153	- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
154	  trigger.

156	  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.

content.content:
17-- Bound an unattended agent's **write surface**, and enforce it from outside the agent. Pre-create the exact file(s) it may edit, tell it to touch nothing else (no new files, no edits to shared code it might be tempted to "improve"), and after it stops, verify the diff in the workflow — reverting anything outside the allowed set rather than trusting the prompt. Prose is a request; the post-hoc diff check is the guarantee, so a misbehaving agent's blast radius is bounded no matter how it strays. Anything the agent would otherwise reach into belongs inlined in its own file (as a source's local helper), not edited in place.
18-- In a multi-stage unattended pipeline, converge **every** failure exit — including an infrastructure failure in a pre-agent setup stage (a fetch, an auth step, scaffolding) — to the same human-triage state as an agent-detected failure. A setup-phase failure that reports itself but leaves the original trigger untouched (e.g. a label still set) makes the item look unprocessed rather than blocked, silently defeating the escalation path. Treat every failure mode as equivalent from the triage perspective.
19-- An unattended agent must **never invoke a tool that surfaces a blocking approval it cannot answer** — there is no human present to click "Allow," so the run stalls indefinitely on step one. The multi-agent-orchestration **Workflow tool is the classic trap**: it mandates an interactive opt-in on *every* run (the prompt only disappears under bypass-permissions / headless modes you cannot rely on the scheduler being in), so a routine that fans out through it hangs before doing any work. Fan out with **plain subagent dispatch** (the Agent/Task tool) instead — it carries no such gate and the orchestrator honors any phase barriers itself — and reserve the Workflow tool for interactive sessions where a human can consent. The general rule: an unattended agent's whole tool path must be answer-free.
20:- **Dispatch a subagent under worktree isolation whenever it may commit.** Without it the child works in the parent's checkout and leaves it wherever it finished — on the child's branch — so the parent's branch-scoped end-of-session checks judge the *child's* commits against the *parent's* transcript and file findings the parent cannot act on. Pass the isolation flag on the dispatch (`isolation: "worktree"`); recovering after the fact means checking the parent back onto its own assigned branch and re-verifying everything.
21-- **A routine that correctly declines has not failed — converge failures, not declines.** When the item a run was dispatched for genuinely cannot be processed (an unreachable source, a dead link, an empty result), record the reason on that item, mark it for human attention, and exit **zero**. Failing the task instead raises a *second* human-triage signal for the same item and reports the pipeline as broken when it in fact judged correctly. Partial success is the same shape: the items that did process still land.
22-- **A run that *skips* its work still exits 0 — a job whose success and whose no-op look identical from outside is telling you nothing.** A scheduler ran green nightly while skipping its main stage on a misread config value, the only trace one skip line in a log nobody opens on a green run. Make every skip state what it skipped and why in the run's own visible output, and confirm a routine works by reading a *reason*, not an exit code: a skip is a finding to triage, not a pass. And when the defect lives inside the mechanism that updates itself (a vendored mount its own maintenance job refreshes, a bootstrap that installs its own successor), the ordinary route can't carry the fix — recognise the self-reference and land the repair out of band rather than waiting for the broken updater.
23-- **The session that designed a judgment stage must not be the one that runs it.** A stage that picks the strongest candidate, ranks a set, or decides what matters has to run in a context that never saw it being built — the designing session knows which candidates it had in mind when it chose the heuristic and will find them again, which is an echo, not judgment. Exercise a freshly-built stage in a subagent whose context starts empty, or leave it to the scheduler. Better, make the clean context **structural rather than remembered**: state it in the task spec as a rule the agent reads every run ("do not load context you were not given — the item's own title, body and discussion are what you have, and they are enough"), so the production path is clean without anyone arranging it.
24-- **A rejected call whose whole purpose was a fallback must be re-issued before you continue.** Arming a timeout wake-up, a watchdog, or a retry is the one class of call whose rejection changes nothing observable: the error scrolls past mid-turn, the run proceeds believing it holds a safety net it never armed, and the gap surfaces only when the primary path dies and nothing recovers it. Read the result of every guard-arming call, re-issue it on the spot, and never claim to be relying on a backstop you didn't confirm.
25-- **Nothing you post to a tracker can be edited — resolve every value before the comment goes up.** The GitHub toolsets these runs use offer comment *creation* and no comment-update tool, so a comment that goes out wrong can only be appended to, leaving the wrong value and its correction both standing forever. An agent session also has **no ambient clock**: a timestamp is only true if you read it (one shell call) rather than filling a placeholder you mean to fix later. Same for every PR number, sha and label a comment asserts — resolve, then post.
26-- **When the outcome your ceiling names is mechanically unavailable, stop short and say so — never substitute a riskier action to close the gap.** A routine told to land work through an auto-merging PR cannot when the repository has auto-merge disabled and its checks will not conclude. The gap looks one command wide, and improvising a merge to close it costs more than the unlanded change does. Where a shared delivery procedure exists (Claudinite's `packs/claudinite-tasks/src/deliver/deliver-pr.md`), the merges it licenses — like the direct merge on a base branch that requires nothing, where the arm is rejected "clean status" by design — are the sanctioned path, not a workaround; anything outside them stays unlanded. An open PR plus a plain statement of what could not be armed and why is a complete, honest result. Re-try the mechanism on each run rather than assuming either state is permanent, and drop the workaround the moment it succeeds.
27-- **A change-gated routine must exclude its *own* writes from its triggers, or it feeds itself.** A routine that commits to, files issues in, or emits artifacts into the same repos it monitors will re-fire on its own output unless every trigger filters it out: its own maintenance commits must not count as "the project changed" (match them by bot-author / `[skip ci]` / a subject convention and exclude — and keep that matcher current with the wording the routine actually writes, or a near-miss silently reads as real work); its own standing-tracker/issue updates must not count as activity (a tracker rewritten every run always sits inside a fixed lookback window, so it re-triggers forever); its own generated plan/report artifact must not count as a repo change. The tell is a routine that fires every cycle on a fleet that is actually quiet. Treat "the routine's inputs never include the routine's outputs" as an invariant when wiring any change-detection signal.
28-- When an unattended routine takes an **irreversible or outward-facing action** (closing an issue, deleting a branch, sending a message), the spec must **define the trigger condition concretely and default to the safe path** — not just name the action. A bare "close if done" invites a wrong close on a superficial match; "close *only* when the ask is verifiably true of the target's current state — else comment" cannot. State what counts as the condition and where to verify it, and make the reversible option (leave it, comment, escalate) the default whenever the check is inconclusive.

## Candidate 1 — land this

**Lesson:** When a subagent is dispatched under worktree isolation (this repo's project-thread flow spins up several in parallel to each implement one approved PR), the isolation guard refuses any Bash call it names git in that's "too complex to verify" it stays inside the worktree — a heredoc, a `&&`-chained command, a pipe, anything combining git with other work. It always names the fix itself ("Split it into plain, separate commands") but the agent has to rediscover this by trial each time rather than composing simple standalone commands up front.

**Evidence:** `2026-09-24T1119Z--pr-846--a85e8b4f-....jsonl` (conversation-logs branch), the single long orchestrating session that implemented PRs #846/#847/#852/#853/#850/#863 via dispatched worktree-isolated subagents. The exact refusal text — "This agent is isolated in the worktree …, but this command is too complex to verify that it stays inside the worktree. Refusing to run it — a worktree-isolated agent's git operations must target its own worktree. Split it into plain, separate commands…" — recurred **28 times** in this one log (e.g. at 08:52:58Z, 08:58:59Z, 09:00:45Z, 09:00:55Z, 09:01:40Z, 09:03:46Z), each time forcing a wasted tool call plus a rewrite into simpler commands (e.g. writing a Python heredoc as a scratch `.py` file and invoking it instead, or dropping `git add -N . 2>/dev/null; git status --short; npm run verify …` into three separate calls).

Not in the local pack's RULES.md, any skill, or `_declined.md`.

**Proposed rung:** terse prose (can't be a declared/coded check — it's about how a live Bash command is composed at runtime, not a property of committed files). This uses 1 of this pass's 2-rule prose ration.

## `merge_pull_request` right after a force-push to its head can 500 - retry, don't diagnose

The PR's mergeable-state recompute lags a force-push to its head branch, so a `merge_pull_request` call issued immediately after can 500 even though the merge is otherwise clean. Treat the first such 500 as a timing artifact and retry with backoff, rather than reading it as a real merge failure.

## Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same commit that deletes what produced its artifacts

Removing a toolchain invites tidying away its ignore rules alongside it — but the artifacts it already produced are usually still sitting untracked in the worktree (`__pycache__/` from an earlier run, `build/` from an earlier build). The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps the junk *into* the commit that was supposed to remove it, and nothing complains: the commit is valid and the tests still pass. Delete (or `git clean`) the artifacts first, then drop their ignore lines. And after any bulk `git add -A`, read `git diff --cached --stat` — staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops telling you about.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/EdFringeNow/.claude/skills/writing-pack-prose

# Writing pack prose

Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.

**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.

## The ration

Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.

- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
  trigger.
- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs on the element's
  provenance file (below).
- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads.
- **Starting a `SKILL.md`, or editing one that declares no body** — say under its frontmatter
  `metadata` what the body is: `body: workflow` for a procedure, whose steps and their gotchas
  change as one, or `body: guidelines` for rules behind a trigger, kept on the skill's one file
  until one has a history of its own. A skill that mixes the two declares the shape of its
  greater part. The harness ignores the key; the corpus's own maintenance reads it, and never
  infers it.

## Shape a rule so it fires

- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
  reader to it.
- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
  to three neighbouring bullets.
- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
  you report the change.
- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
  it.
- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
  hand-built command.
- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
  reader doesn't need at act time goes on the element's provenance file (below).
- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
  teaches a world the reader won't find.
- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.

## The provenance log - where a rule's rationale lives

A pack keeps one file per element under `provenance/`, beside its `RULES.md`: an append-only
log of the decisions behind the element, read by maintenance and review - the pass that asks
whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written - and never by a session.
No rule sends its reader there, nothing loads it, and it never vendors: a member mounting a
canon pack receives the rules, not the reasoning behind them. The grammar, the kinds, the
fields and the tool are [changing-pack-elements](../changing-pack-elements/SKILL.md)'s; what
this skill adds is how a rule is written so the log can hold it.

- **Ending a rule** - every rule in a `RULES.md` ends with the bare marker naming its file -
  `… never a filesystem walk. (url-filter-host-operators)` - and nothing else: don't name the
  folder, don't link it, don't ask the reader to follow anything. The marker is the element's
  id: two to four hyphenated words for the guideline rather than its wording, chosen once and
  never renamed, so a rewording never touches it and a member's override can name it. Two
  rules whose history is one may share a marker. A guidelines skill's bullets are the skill's
  file's and carry none, until one's history diverges and it takes a marker and a file of its
  own; a workflow skill's steps carry none, the skill being the element.
- **Adding a rule** - write the brief rule and end it with its marker; create its file with a
  `born` entry through `provenance.mjs append` (`mark` creates the file where none exists),
  and put the reason there, never in the rule. A consequence the reader needs under pressure
  earns its clause; rationale the reader doesn't need at act time is the entry's. Write the
  entry so a future review can **reaffirm the rule from it** - `Retire when` is what would
  have to be true for the rule to go.
  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
    the error, the measured cost).
  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it - in a member's
    local pack; a canon file carries the paraphrase, never the quote.
- **Rewording, moving, splitting or converting a rule** - the entry is owed in the same
  change, and the forced skill names its kind.
- **A check's rationale** - on the check's own file, named by its id (`cer/version-bumped` →
  `cer-version-bumped.md`); nothing is added to the check.
- **Removing a rule or check** - its file stays and gains a `retired` entry as its last, in
  the same change.

The `provenance-integrity` check holds the mechanism together - every carrier names a live
file, every file parses - and `provenance-change-recorded` holds the change: a carrier that
changed lands with its entry. A pack not yet on the convention is put there by
`provenance.mjs mark`, and its history filled by the
[backfilling-provenance](../backfilling-provenance/SKILL.md) skill; nothing here is done rule by
rule.

## Evidence

The commit and its PR remain the archive - the story of the incident, quoted exchanges and
session ids live there and in the capture, never in the rule and never in a canon's log. What
an entry takes from them is only the **reaffirmable core**: `Source` and `Reason`, the minimum
a future review needs to re-test the rule, and `Retire when`, the test it is reaffirmed
against. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument - a cost
the reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/EdFringeNow/.claude/skills/changing-pack-elements

# Changing a pack's elements

A pack's carriers - the rules in `RULES.md`, a skill and its triggers, a coded or declared
check, a task and its policy, the manifest - say *what* a session does. The decision behind
each - why it reads so, who decided, from what evidence, why this carrier and this trigger,
what was rejected, what would retire it - is one append-only file per element under the
pack's `provenance/`, read by maintenance and never by a session. Three things follow for
any edit under a pack.

## 1. The edit owes an entry, in the same change

Every change to what a carrier decides lands with an entry on the element's file, and the
`provenance-change-recorded` check says so again at the Stop hook when it did not. Which
file: the marker that ends a rule or guideline names it (`(url-filter-host-operators)` →
`provenance/url-filter-host-operators.md`), and two carriers may name one file while their
history is one; an unmarked guideline's is its skill's; a skill's is its directory name; a
check's its id with `/` as `-`; a task's its id; the manifest's `_pack.md`. Which kind:

| The change | Kind |
|---|---|
| a rule, guideline, skill body or step reads differently | `reworded` - or `strengthened` / `weakened` when the modality moved |
| a rule split in two, or two folded into one | `split` / `merged` (an entry on every file involved) |
| a guideline given a file of its own, its history having diverged from its skill's | `split` on the skill's file, `born` on the bullet's, with `Mechanism` |
| a rule moved to another carrier or pack | `moved`, with `Mechanism` |
| prose turned into a check | `converted`, with `Mechanism` and the deletion-test verdict |
| a skill's description or `force-load-on-*` trigger | `trigger-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a task's preconditions, `expected_outcome`, `automerge`, model or worker | `policy-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a check's severity, or the gate deciding when it fires | `severity-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| what an element applies to, where its text reads the same - a manifest's `requires` or fingerprint, a check's file scope, a skill's corpus | `scope-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a new element | `born`, with `Mechanism` - and `mark` first if the carrier has no file |
| an element removed | `retired` - the file stays, and this is its last entry |
| a review that found new evidence or changed the retire test | `reaffirmed`; a review that found nothing new writes nothing |

No entry is owed for whitespace, a re-wrap, a code comment in a check, a fixture, a test, a
README row, a version bump, or the marking pass's own markers and `body:` lines.

Write the entry in the file grammar and append it through the tool, which validates it and
refuses one that carries a secret:

```
node packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs append <pack> <element> <<'EOF'
## 2026-09-21 · reworded · the consequence clause said why twice (#2210)
- **Reason:** the second sentence restated the rule; cut.
- **Actor:** @handle (owner).
- **Model:** <the model this session runs, as the harness names it>
- **Landed:** #2210
EOF
```

In a member the tool is `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs`, and
the pack is under `.claudinite/local/packs/`. `--changed` in place of the element appends the
same entry to every element the working tree's diff touched - a sweep's one-line entries.
The fields, each written only where there is something behind it: `Source`, `Reason`,
`Actor` (the person by handle with their role, or the run and who merged it - never an
email), `Model`, `Mechanism` (the carrier and its trigger, and why - required on `born`,
`converted`, `moved`, `trigger-changed`, `policy-changed`, `severity-changed`), `Rejected`,
`Retire when`, `Landed`. An entry never restates the rule: the carrier is the description,
the entry is the decision. A candidate turned down goes on `_declined.md` the same way, kind
`declined`, with `Source`, `Reason` and `Actor`.

**Size the entry to the decision, never to the work.** Most are three to five lines. Each
field is the shortest answer that is still an answer, and one clause is usually the whole of
one - `Reason: the folder never existed.` Where a required `Mechanism` keeps the carrier it
already had, the new value is the whole of it - `a regex` - and the why-clause is owed only
where the choice of carrier was itself the decision. The diff, the commit message and the
pull request already hold what changed, how it was proved and what it cost; an entry
retelling any of them writes the record twice and buries the line a review came for. Length
is earned only by a decision that was weighed - an alternative turned down, a constraint that
forced the shape - so a corrected path, a repointed pattern or a renamed field gets one line,
and a change nobody deliberated over gets `Reason` alone. Cut a field rather than pad it, and
cut one that repeats another field or the entry's own title.

A file is meant to grow: a wrong entry is answered by a later one, never by editing the one
that was wrong. The check advises against a line lost or altered and refuses nothing.

### The one lane that writes the past

`append` and `apply` are append-only, and the tool enforces it: an entry dated before the
file's last is refused, because a change being recorded now cannot have happened before the
change recorded last. **The backfill is the deliberate exception**, and `--backfill` on
either command is how it says so. It is deriving a history that already happened, so its
entries are dated in the past by definition, and under that flag the file is re-rendered in
date order rather than appended to. Two things only it may do:

- **Replace what the references conversion wrote.** A file the conversion filled carries a
  `born` dated by the conversion write rather than by the element. Where the derived birth
  is earlier, that placeholder is what is being corrected and the tool drops it, naming it
  in the run's output; where the placeholder's date *is* the birth, no earlier born arrives
  and it stands. The dates decide, so neither truncating these files as a class nor leaving
  them is the rule. Only the conversion's own entry is ever replaced - an entry somebody
  wrote is never dropped, whatever its date.
- **Open a file the marking pass could not.** An element retired *before* that pass is named
  by no carrier, so nothing will ever create its file. A `--backfill` batch that opens with
  `born` creates it; its whole history, birth through `retired`, arrives at once or not at
  all. Do not put such a history on `_pack.md` instead: a `retired` entry seals the file it
  ends, and `_pack.md` is the one file in a pack that must stay appendable forever.

Every other caller - every change being made now - uses the plain lane, where a file only
ever grows at its end.

## 2. The README carries use, never history

A pack's `README.md` is for the person adopting the pack or reaching for one of its
elements: when the pack activates, what each check demands and what satisfies it, when a
skill is the thing to load, what the task does to the repository, and the catalog of what
the pack carries. Never how an element came to be, what it replaced, why its id reads as it
does, what an earlier shape did, or how the pack is maintained. The test is the sentence: a
date, a pull request number, an "until", a "was", a "kept as it was" or a "distilled from"
is a decision, and a decision is an entry on the element's file - `_pack.md` for the pack's
own shape. Move it there; do not write it here.

## 3. The mount is never edited

A file under `.claudinite/shared/` arrived from a canon and the next converge replaces the
whole tree. Change it in the canon, or carry the difference in the repo's own
`.claudinite/local/packs/`.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# edfringe-now — this repo's own rules

Lessons this repo paid for once. A lesson that would hold in another repo belongs in the
Claudinite canon instead. The data pipeline's rules are the `data-pipeline` skill and the
requirements harness's are the `requirements-harness` skill; each loads when its paths are edited.

## Delivering work

- **Asking how to fix a structural or architectural complaint via `AskUserQuestion`** — offer
  restructuring itself as one option, not only mechanism-level tweaks to the existing shape; the
  owner's free-text answers have named the restructure nobody offered.
  (askuserquestion-structural-option)

- **Opening a PR for a work item's own issue** (a bot-filed `[claudinite-work]` item or a person's
  marked ad-hoc issue) — reference it without `Closes #N`: GitHub's auto-close beats
  `converge-item.mjs` and leaves the issue closed but still wearing its live status label.
  (never-closes-n-own-issue)

- **Writing a PR body** — this repo has no PR template, so write it from the commit message
  without searching for one. (no-pr-template)

- **Reaching for `verify-in-production` after merging a change to what the site renders or
  does** — file nothing: the goldens, `npm run test:ui` and a look at the served page run before
  the merge. Reserve it for non-user-facing infra whose effect first appears in a deploy, a
  scheduler slot or a CI lane. (verify-in-production-infra-only)

- **Writing a duration or before/after number into a commit or PR body** — compute it from real
  timestamps, never a felt sense of elapsed time around unconsumed background sleeps.
  (measured-duration-real-timestamps)

- **Landing a lesson that tells a session to retry, ignore or explain away a permission, security
  or classifier denial** — don't, however much retry evidence backs it: a checked-in rule is a
  standing bypass every unattended session loads. Report a recurring denial to the owner instead.
  (no-denial-bypass-rules)

## Verifying a change

- **Calling a change under `site/` or the requirements fixtures done** — run `npm run test:ui`
  locally: `npm run verify` never compares the goldens, and CI's `ui-requirements` lane skips them
  on a diff outside `site/` and `product/`. (test-ui-before-pixel-change)

- **Verifying a UI change** — look at it: serve `site/` (not the repo root) with
  `python3 -m http.server 8000` and drive `http://localhost:8000` with the preinstalled
  Chromium; the pages fetch their data, so a `file://` open fails. For `/plan`, a slug-per-line
  text file works as a favourites list. (serve-site-to-look)

- **Scripting Playwright** — import the global build by its ESM entry and launch with no
  `executablePath`; `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` already points at the matching browser.
  (launch-playwright-executablepath)

  ```js
  import { chromium } from '/opt/node22/lib/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs';
  ```

- **A bare `import 'playwright'` failing with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`** — use the absolute import
  above rather than `npm i playwright`: a fresh install pulls a newer Playwright that wants a
  browser build the image doesn't ship, and in the repo root it dirties `package.json`.
  (npm-playwright-scratchpad)

- **The Now page throwing `L is not defined` under Playwright** — Leaflet loads from `unpkg.com`,
  which the browser can't reach here; route `https://unpkg.com/**` to the matching file in
  `product/requirements/shared/harness/vendor/leaflet/` before navigating. (site-index-htmls)

- **Asserting a driven page logged no errors** — filter failed requests to off-box hosts (Google
  Fonts, map tiles, anything the browser can't tunnel to); they fail on every run and are not
  application errors. (known-noisy-console)

- **A "the live site shows wrong data" report** — ask first for screenshots of DevTools' Network
  tab and Application → Cache Storage panel, before building a local repro: three caching layers
  can produce the identical symptom, and only the browser's evidence says which is in play.
  (live-data-bug-browser-evidence)

## The sandbox and its network

- **About to report a capability as unavailable** — probe it in this session first, whatever
  this file says; the egress policy changes from day to day. (report-capability-unavailable)

  ```sh
  curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" --max-time 15 https://<host>/
  ```

- **Reading a 403 from the proxy** — `curl -v` tells you whose it is: `CONNECT tunnel failed,
  response 403` is a policy denial, the same code after a negotiated tunnel is the origin
  refusing you. `curl -sS "$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status"` lists recent policy rejections.
  (reading-403-proxy)

- **Checking what the deployed site serves** — `curl https://www.edfringenow.com/…` rather than
  reasoning from the working tree, but the response is CDN-cached: re-check after a delay before
  reading a stale 200 as a failed deploy. (checking-deployed-site)

- **Needing a screenshot of an off-box site headless Chromium can't tunnel to** — route every
  request through `page.route('**/*', …)` fulfilled by `curl`, where the probe shows `curl`
  reaches the host. (offsite-screenshot-via-curl)

- **Building a command or poll on `gh`** — it is not installed here; use the GitHub MCP tools,
  and never suppress a poll condition's stderr, which is what would have said so.
  (no-gh-cli)

## GitHub and CI

- **Calling `actions_list` for workflow runs** — always pass `perPage`; without it the call
  overflows the tool-result limit on this repo's history. (actionslist-listworkflowruns-overflows)

- **Checking whether a PR merged via `list_pull_requests`** — read `merged_at` for non-null; the
  `merged` field decodes `false` even for a merged PR. (listpullrequestss-merged-field)

- **`pull_request_read method=get_files` overflowing** — retry at a smaller `perPage` (10 works
  where 100 overflows), or answer from `get` plus `get_commits`. (pullrequestread-method-getfiles)

- **A CI job stuck `queued` until it auto-cancels, or dying in "Prepare all required actions"** —
  that is a GitHub outage, not this PR's failure: say what local `verify`/`test:ui` covers, and
  don't recommend waiting it out. (ci-infra-outage-tells)

- **A `[claudinite-task]` needs-human issue piling up bot comments** — the watchdog is nagging
  about one unexecuted slot, not reporting a recurring failure; count what landed
  (`git log --grep=<worker's commit subject>`) and read that slot's job log before shipping a fix.
  (needs-human-one-slot)

## The site's code

- **Writing behaviour more than one page needs** — put it in `site/shared/` and import it from
  each page; never copy it. `site/plan/lib/`'s DOM-free engine (`engine.js`, `travel.js`,
  `itinerary.js`, `availability.js`) is shared with `site/planNG/`, so it never learns one
  festival's specifics. (cross-page-in-shared)

## Product research and design

- **Researching a competitor for a `wiki-growth` pass** — fetch the competitor's page first, and
  fall back to `WebSearch` only once the fetch fails, citing the snippet's publisher.
  (competitor-fetch-first)

- **Dispatching a research subagent for a long, multi-round wiki pass** — give it an explicit
  budget ("finish with a few NOT FOUNDs rather than dig exhaustively"): a subagent killed
  mid-run hands back no report at all. (research-subagent-budget)

- **Building a first-pass UI/UX mockup** — default to graphics-first, minimal-text, wizard-style
  screens that hide answered questions; the owner rejects generic buttons-and-prose screens.
  (mockup-graphics-first)

content.content:
1	---
2	name: prose-to-checks
3	description: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
4	metadata:
5	  body: workflow
6	  usage:
7	    expect: judgment
8	---
9	
10	# Convert existing prose to checks
11	
12	A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs: prose that is always-testable but was never converted
13	becomes a check, so the packs keep shedding context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is
14	first learned.
15	
16	## The corpus is the caller's, the method is this skill's
17	
18	**This skill never decides which packs to read.** A caller says that — a task's `task.md`, or whoever
19	asked — and the two shapes it comes in differ only in how wide the prose is:
20	
21	- **The upgrade pass**, as the last step of a
22	  [growth-extract](../../tasks/growth-extract/task.md) run: the scope is the prose **that run just
23	  wrote**. Extraction already descends the promotion ladder per lesson, but a lesson written as prose
24	  under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides, so it gets asked once more before the
25	  PR opens. Never widen from here into the standing backlog.
26	- **A standing sweep** over a named corpus: everything under it — each pack's `RULES.md`, and any
27	  `SKILL.md` beside them — whatever was converted before. A sweep holds no state between runs.
28	
29	Plus on demand, when someone asks. Everything below is identical for every caller.
30	
31	## First gate — a working rule, not a product statement
32	
33	Before asking whether a rule is *testable*, ask whether it belongs to a pack at all: **does it govern
34	how we work, or state what the product does?** A pack — canon or local — homes the conventions,
35	gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks whatever the feature happens to be. A rule
36	asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or that a feature's parts are wired to
37	each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable spec and the suite that proves
38	it.
39	
40	This gate comes **first** because product statements sail through the check-the-world test below —
41	"this module must export `X`" has an obvious static signature. Converting one splits a feature's
42	definition across two systems and lands half of it in the one no test of the product ever reads.
43	Load-bearingness is not the test: a real gap in product coverage is a *requirements* gap. Neither is build
44	quality — a product statement converts into a genuinely well-made check, clean parse and see-it-fail proof and
45	all, and is still the wrong kind. The discriminator, applied **before** you write anything: *if the product
46	changed its mind tomorrow, would this rule be wrong?* Wrong → it's a requirement, and a red check would report
47	a product decision as a process violation. Still true whatever the product decides → it's a working rule.
48

1	---
2	name: growth-dedup
3	description: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
4	metadata:
5	  body: workflow
6	  usage:
7	    expect: judgment
8	---
9	
10	# Dedup local packs against the canon
11	
12	Prune a repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) of items the canon it consumes now
13	covers. Often there is nothing to prune, and that is a finished run, not a failed one. Run under the
14	unattended [growth-dedup task](../../tasks/growth-dedup/task.md), that task frames dispatch, the
15	human-gated PR and the tracking issue.
16	
17	**The yardstick is the mounted canon** — the exact revision the repo currently consumes, what
18	`.claudinite/shared/` holds at the mount's stamp — never a live fetch (a promotion is visible
19	here only once baselining has converged the mount to include it). The mount is never a prune
20	*target*, only what you prune *against*.
21	
22	## Start from the canon's diff, not the canon
23	
24	Reconciling a local pack against a whole canon is a search with no shape: most canon lines have been there
25	for months, and if they were going to cover a local item they mostly already did on an earlier pass. What
26	makes an item newly prunable is a canon **change**. So when the reconciliation has a window, work its diff
27	before reading any local pack. The unattended run is handed that diff — its code-work writes the window's canon
28	additions into the task's tracking issue — and an owner asking in-session can usually name a window ("since we
29	last did this") and read it the same way. Either way, the candidate list is:
30	
31	- **Added prose lines** — each is a canon rule that did not exist last pass. Ask of each: which local item
32	  was carrying this point in this repo's own names?
33	- **Added or widened checks** — a new id in a pack's `declared-checks.json`, a new check module, or a
34	  widened `scanFiles`/`matchLines` on an existing one. These are the strongest coverage there is (see below),
35	  and they are invisible in the prose corpus, so a prose-only read of the window misses them entirely.
36	- **Rewordings** — the canon stating an idea it already had in different words. These prune nothing; they
37	  are what the **rephrase** action below tracks.
38	- **Removed canon lines** — the reverse signal. Coverage the canon just *dropped* can never justify a prune,
39	  and a local item the canon used to cover has become load-bearing. Never prune against a `-` line.
40	
41	The diff sets the run's *focus*, never its permission: a local item covered by an older line in a changed
42	pack is still a legitimate prune when you can quote that line. Working the diff first just means the run
43	spends its attention where the new coverage actually is.
44	
45	## The three actions — every one removes portable text
46	
47	- **Remove** a now-duplicated local item, since the canon is the single source of truth for
48	  portable rules.
49	- **Strip** a *partially* covered item down to its residue — when an item's general half is now
50	  canon-owned but it still carries a stronger point about a narrower case, **delete the portable
51	  half in place and keep only the residue**. A strip is a **deletion that shrinks the entry**:
52	  lead with the residual point (using the file's own `(canon)` tag convention if it has one),
53	  never with a meta-line like "this rule is portable (canon)", and **never re-state the
54	  now-canon rule, its fix, or which pack owns it** — carrying it is exactly what you are
55	  removing. If your "strip" adds words or restates the canon, you have *un*-deduped the item:
56	  keep the pre-edit text instead.
57	- **Rephrase** a local procedure *only* when the canon's wording of the same idea has changed,
58	  so the local packs stay consistent with the canon they point at — a rephrase tracks a wording
59	  drift; it never grows the entry and never re-imports canon prose.
60	
61	An edit that leaves an entry the same size or larger, re-quotes the now-canon rule, or names the
62	owning pack's fix is a **corruption, not a dedup**. When in doubt about a kept item, leave it
63	byte-for-byte unchanged rather than "reconcile" its wording. The `dedup-prune-integrity` check
64	([dedup-integrity.mjs](../../workRules/dedup-integrity.mjs)) is the machine backstop: it reds the session
65	when a dedup-labeled commit grows a local-pack prose file, or when any change adds a line that
66	restates a canon rule.
67	
68	## The keep-test: says *more*, not merely says it more specifically
69	
70	Every local item is more specific than the canon, so specificity alone is never the test.
71	Distinguish two cases:
72	
73	- **The general rule in local dress** — it makes the canon's point but leans on this repo's
74	  classes, files, or names to make it. Once the canon covers the point, those names were only
75	  illustration: prune it.
76	- **A stronger point about a narrower case** — it asserts something the canon's general rule
77	  leaves out: a tighter constraint, a sharper claim that holds for this repo's narrower
78	  situation. Keep it.
79	
80	So ask not "is it specific" (it always is) but "does it only lean on specific names to make the
81	general point, or does it make a point the canon doesn't?" Prune the first; keep the second.
82	
83	## A canon check covers an item too — and more strongly than prose
84	
85	The canon carries rules as **conformance checks**, not only prose. A local item is covered when
86	a canon check *enforces* it — stronger coverage than a stated line, since the rule runs on every
87	session and CI pass. Consult the machine-readable rule catalog
88	(`node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs --list`: id, severity, description,
89	doc pointer — it lists the active local packs' own checks too) alongside the prose corpus, and
90	when a check covers the item, **quote the rule id** where you'd otherwise quote a canon line.
91	This cuts both ways: a **local pack's own check** is redundant once a canon check enforces the
92	same rule — prune the local `.mjs` (and drop it from `pack.mjs` + its fixture) exactly as you'd
93	prune a duplicated prose line. The keep-test above is unchanged.
94	
95	## Discipline
96	
97	- **Only remove a local item you can show the mounted canon genuinely covers — quote the canon
98	  line (or the covering check's rule id).** When unsure, leave it; a wrongful prune deletes a
99	  real local lesson.
100	- **Write only inside the local packs.** A dedup run's whole surface is
101	  `.claudinite/local/packs/` — never the canon it prunes against, never the project's own code. The
102	  `growth-write-scope` check ([growth-write-scope.mjs](../../workRules/growth-write-scope.mjs)) keys on the
103	  run's pinned `Claudinite growth: dedup local packs` title and reds any path outside that surface.
104	- **Record each prune on the element's provenance file**, in the same change, through
105	  `provenance.mjs append`: `retired` (superseded by the canon element it names) for a removal -
106	  the file stays - `weakened` for a strip, `reworded` for a rephrase; the changing-pack-elements
107	  skill has the grammar.
108	- If an edit touches something a test reads, run the repo's offline test suite and keep it green
109	  before delivering.

  never with a meta-line like "this rule is portable (canon)", and **never re-state the
  now-canon rule, its fix, or which pack owns it** — carrying it is exactly what you are
  removing. If your "strip" adds words or restates the canon, you have *un*-deduped the item:
  keep the pre-edit text instead.
- **Rephrase** a local procedure *only* when the canon's wording of the same idea has changed,
  so the local packs stay consistent with the canon they point at — a rephrase tracks a wording
  drift; it never grows the entry and never re-imports canon prose.

An edit that leaves an entry the same size or larger, re-quotes the now-canon rule, or names the
owning pack's fix is a **corruption, not a dedup**. When in doubt about a kept item, leave it
byte-for-byte unchanged rather than "reconcile" its wording. The `dedup-prune-integrity` check
([dedup-integrity.mjs](../../workRules/dedup-integrity.mjs)) is the machine backstop: it reds the session
when a dedup-labeled commit grows a local-pack prose file, or when any change adds a line that
restates a canon rule.

## The keep-test: says *more*, not merely says it more specifically

Every local item is more specific than the canon, so specificity alone is never the test.
Distinguish two cases:

- **The general rule in local dress** — it makes the canon's point but leans on this repo's
  classes, files, or names to make it. Once the canon covers the point, those names were only
  illustration: prune it.
- **A stronger point about a narrower case** — it asserts something the canon's general rule
  leaves out: a tighter constraint, a sharper claim that holds for this repo's narrower
  situation. Keep it.

So ask not "is it specific" (it always is) but "does it only lean on specific names to make the
general point, or does it make a point the canon doesn't?" Prune the first; keep the second.

## A canon check covers an item too — and more strongly than prose

The canon carries rules as **conformance checks**, not only prose. A local item is covered when
a canon check *enforces* it — stronger coverage than a stated line, since the rule runs on every
session and CI pass. Consult the machine-readable rule catalog
(`node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs --list`: id, severity, description,
doc pointer — it lists the active local packs' own checks too) alongside the prose corpus, and
when a check covers the item, **quote the rule id** where you'd otherwise quote a canon line.
This cuts both ways: a **local pack's own check** is redundant once a canon check enforces the
same rule — prune the local `.mjs` (and drop it from `pack.mjs` + its fixture) exactly as you'd
prune a duplicated prose line. The keep-test above is unchanged.

## Discipline

- **Only remove a local item you can show the mounted canon genuinely covers — quote the canon
  line (or the covering check's rule id).** When unsure, leave it; a wrongful prune deletes a
  real local lesson.
- **Write only inside the local packs.** A dedup run's whole surface is
  `.claudinite/local/packs/` — never the canon it prunes against, never the project's own code. The
  `growth-write-scope` check ([growth-write-scope.mjs](../../workRules/growth-write-scope.mjs)) keys on the
  run's pinned `Claudinite growth: dedup local packs` title and reds any path outside that surface.
- **Record each prune on the element's provenance file**, in the same change, through
  `provenance.mjs append`: `retired` (superseded by the canon element it names) for a removal -
  the file stays - `weakened` for a strip, `reworded` for a rephrase; the changing-pack-elements
  skill has the grammar.
- If an edit touches something a test reads, run the repo's offline test suite and keep it green
  before delivering.

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking.
- **Reference the issue, when the change has one** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where
  the commit finishes it. A change tracked by its PR alone references nothing.
- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever

1	# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request
2	
3	How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
4	delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
5	run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
6	the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
7	your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
8	lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.
9	
10	## The branch and the pull request were chosen for you
11	
12	**Push to the `Target-branch:` your item carries, and onto the `Target-pr:` where it
13	carries one.** The executor resolved both from the task's `expected_outcome` before
14	your session started: `fresh_pr` gave you a new branch and left the task's earlier pull
15	requests alone; `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` gave you the branch of the task's
16	newest open pull request, or a fresh one only where the task had no open pull request
17	at all; `supersede_existing_pr` gave you a fresh branch and listed the earlier ones under
18	`Supersedes:`. Where there is a `Target-pr:`, push onto it and open nothing — the pull
19	request already exists and your push updates it. Where there is none, open your pull
20	request on that branch. Never mint a branch name, never search for an open pull
21	request to reuse, and never close an earlier run's pull request yourself: the converge
22	(`src/session/converge-item.mjs`, handed `--pr`) closes what `Supersedes:` names once yours
23	exists, and a run that delivered nothing leaves them where they were.
24	
25	**A `Target-pr:` that conflicts with its base is yours to resolve, not to walk away
26	from.** Merge the base branch into the target branch, resolve the conflicts, and carry
27	on with your own work on top - a task told to amend has no prerogative to open a second
28	pull request, and one that forks leaves the first open and accumulating beside the
29	second. If you cannot resolve it, stop and say so in your wrap-up comment: a parked item
30	naming the conflict is a correct outcome, and a second pull request is not one.
31	
32	## Say which task wrote it
33	
34	**Every commit you push on a task's behalf carries `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` on
35	its own line** — the pack and task id from the work item's first line. When you merge,
36	put the same line in the squash commit's message too: the merge commit is what lands on
37	the default branch, and it is the one the signal collectors read.
38	
39	That trailer is how the scheduler tells the project moving from the machinery running. A
40	task's own delivery must never count as the repo activity that wakes the next task, and
41	a title is not a reliable way to say so — every new task's title is a new leak. Yours
42	says it in the commit.
43	
44	## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest
45	
46	Your task's declared `automerge` is a **ceiling, not a plan**.
47	On a request item the authorization is the item's **`Merge:` field** instead,
48	read within that ceiling: absent means `nothing`, `if-narrow` means the
49	`narrow-diff` composite, and any other value is the policy expression itself.
50	Whichever source it came from:
51	
52	- **`nothing`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
53	  applies to you.
54	- **`anything`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
55	  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
56	  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
57	- **a policy list** (e.g. `['comment-only-changes', 'readme-changes']`, a folder
58	  scope such as `['under:product-wiki']`, or an intersection of the two,
59	  `['under:product-wiki && doc-changes']`) — the task may
60	  land its PR only when the diff sits inside the policy, and the policy engine decides
61	  that, never your reading of the diff. Before step 2, run it from the repository root —
62	  `src/session/merge-policy-run.mjs` in the claudinite-tasks pack (probe
63	  `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/src/session/merge-policy-run.mjs`, falling back to
64	  `packs/claudinite-tasks/src/session/merge-policy-run.mjs` in the canon):
65	
66	  ```
67	  node <that file> --base <the PR's base branch> --policy '<the terms, ;-joined>'
68	  ```
69	
70	  `AUTOMERGE: no` — leave the PR open for review, quote the verdict line in your wrap-up,
71	  and stop; a diff wider than its policy waiting for a person is a correct outcome, and
72	  you never re-shape a change to fit the classifier. `AUTOMERGE: yes` — amend your
73	  branch's final commit to carry the arming trailer on its own line,
74	  `Claudinite-Automerge-Policy: <the same expression>`, push, and continue below (the
75	  `automerge-policy-scope` check re-measures the diff against the trailer, so a
76	  mis-measured arm goes red instead of merging).
77	
78	## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference
79	
80	`.claudinite-settings.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:
81	
82	- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
83	- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
84	  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading an
85	  authorized landing to review is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
86	- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
87	  materializing it is the update converge's job, not yours.
88	- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
89	  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
90	  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the work item.
91	
92	## 2. Arm auto-merge
93	
94	Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
95	it once this repo's required checks pass.
96	
97	## 3. When the arm is rejected
98	
99	- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
100	  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
101	  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
102	  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
103	  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
104	- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
105	  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
106	  PR's **head sha**:
107	  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
108	    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
109	  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
110	    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
111	  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
112	    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
113	    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
114	    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
115	    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
116	    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
117	    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the ceiling — the trail
118	    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
119	    unseen check does not survive anything.
120	
121	## Never
122	
123	Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
124	arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
125	manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
126	are always legal outcomes.
